questions.prompt: What's the Core Web Vitals threshold for a 'good' LCP at p75 of real users?
questions.explanation: LCP ≤ 2.5s is 'good'. 2.5-4.0s is 'needs improvement'. > 4.0s is 'poor'. The threshold is measured at p75 of your real users — hitting it for half your users isn't enough.

questions.prompt: When does wrapping a component in React.memo actually help performance?

options.label: Always — memo prevents all unnecessary renders
When the component uses useState
When the parent re-renders frequently AND the child receives the same props on most renders AND the child's render is expensive enough that the prop comparison saves more than it costs
When the component returns a large JSX tree

questions.explanation: All three preconditions matter. Memo's only job is to skip render when props are shallowly equal — that requires the parent to frequently re-render, the props to often be the same (which means stable callbacks via useCallback, stable objects via useMemo), and a render expensive enough that the comparison overhead pays off. Miss any condition and memo is dead weight.

questions.prompt: Your INP regressed from 180ms to 420ms after a feature shipped. What's the best first investigation?

options.label: Wrap every component in React.memo

Profile the interaction in DevTools Performance to find long tasks on the main thread, then break them up — yield to the main thread with scheduler.yield(), useTransition for heavy renders, or move work to requestIdleCallback
Add more useMemo to derived values
Switch to a different state management library

questions.explanation: INP regressions come from long tasks blocking the main thread during interactions. The fix is to find the long task (DevTools Performance shows it as a red-cornered block ≥ 50ms), then break it up — yield between chunks, mark heavy renders as transitions, or defer non-urgent work. Memo and library swaps without profiling are performance theatre.

questions.prompt: Why does moment.js bloat bundles so much?

options.label: It's written in TypeScript and TS adds runtime overhead
It uses Object.assign which doesn't minify well
It doesn't tree-shake (CommonJS-style internals) and ships all locales by default, so importing one function pulls in the entire library plus every locale
It loads timezone data from a CDN

questions.explanation: moment is ~67KB gzipped even if you use one function, because its module structure prevents tree-shaking and it bundles all locales by default. date-fns and dayjs are ESM, tree-shakeable, and ~5-10KB for typical usage. The swap is mechanical and one of the highest-ROI bundle fixes in any older React codebase.

questions.prompt: An SSR React app shows a console warning 'Text content does not match server-rendered HTML'. What's typically the cause?

options.label: The server is running an older React version than the client
The HTML emitted by the server is malformed

The first client render produced different output than the server render — common culprits include date/time formatting using local timezone, Math.random() or non-stable IDs, conditional rendering based on window/localStorage, or third-party scripts mutating the DOM before hydration
The Suspense fallback didn't render fast enough

questions.explanation: Hydration mismatch = server's HTML and client's first render disagree. React throws away the SSR work and re-renders from scratch — you pay the SSR cost AND lose its benefit. The cures are about determinism: render the same content on server and client, defer client-only logic to useEffect (which runs after hydration), use useId for stable IDs, and keep third-party scripts off the critical path.
